attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own essay, written in his voice.

semantics.note: The causal chain is captured: subsidized subscriptions shielded users from costs and built inefficient habits, which became a problem once billing changed. 'Always going to be a problem' supports adding the later-problems link.

contract.note: Reading the claim as a broad behavioural claim about enterprise customers is fair and ordinary. The criteria require a causal link, not just a price gap, and that suits a causal claim.

evidence.note: Dated 13 June 2026, before the post. It shows subscriptions were cheaper than API access and loss-making at high use, but it does not measure learned inefficiency or a causal effect on later spending.
April 2026 preprint (v1). It shows large technical variation in token use across models and runs. That is an alternative explanation for spending problems, not a test of subscription-induced habits.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no matched customer study or billing record showing that subscriptions reduced attention to cost or caused the later billing problems. e1 shows a price gap only. e2 points to technical causes that would need to be controlled for. The evidence settles neither the support condition nor the contradiction condition.

attribution.note: Zitron calls the proposition 'the truth', so he adopts it as his own. It is his gloss, not a quote from Macdonald.

semantics.note: It keeps the universal 'nobody' and 'any ROI', and properly leaves out the rhetorical 'permission' framing.

contract.note: This is firm, universal wording, so a plain reading is appropriate. Counting a credible survey of quantified realized ROI as a demonstration, while noting its self-reported limits, is an ordinary reading of 'show any ROI'. The result depends on accepting that standard.

evidence.note: An Omdia survey of 2,050 practitioners, published by Snowflake in March 2026, before the post. Respondents who quantified their ROI reported $1.49 back per $1 invested. It is vendor-hosted and self-reported, but it does document realized returns.

PwC's independent survey, January 2026. 56% of CEOs reported no financial return, but about 30% reported higher revenue and 26% lower costs. That backs the idea that returns are widely elusive, not universally absent, though it is not net ROI.

reviews.rationale: The universal claim fails if any credible record shows realized ROI before 15 June 2026. The Omdia/Snowflake survey publicly reported quantified positive returns per dollar invested before the post. PwC's independent survey also found a minority reporting revenue or cost gains. Self-reporting weakens the evidence but does not rescue 'nobody'. Zitron's point that returns are broadly elusive is reasonable; the universal wording is not.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own essay.

semantics.note: 'There is no reversing this trend' is firm and has no deadline. Treating it as an open-ended negative forecast about both labs' economics is fair. The fundraising clause is reasoning, not a condition.

contract.note: The evaluator chose the two-quarter persistence test and inferred what 'this trend' refers to; the contract says so openly. One profitable quarter cannot refute the claim, which is consistent with Zitron's own warning about a single profitable quarter. The standard is reasonable.

evidence.note: Anthropic's S-1, filed 26 October 2026, before the evaluation date. It reports Q2 2026 GAAP operating income and efficiency gains, but establishes only one profitable quarter. It is unaudited and warns margins may shrink as compute expands. It does not meet the early-resolution rule.
FT, August 2026. It reports customers capping usage and labs cutting prices, so price sensitivity continues. That is consistent with the claim but cannot show the trend will never reverse.

reviews.rationale: The forecast has no deadline. Neither early-resolution trigger is met: there is no evidence of two consecutive quarters covering full costs, and neither company has failed for good. Anthropic's single profitable quarter is material but not enough. The evidence available by the cutoff does not settle the forecast.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words; 'they' refers to the AI tools organizations are paying for.

semantics.note: All three assertions are kept: not replacing anyone, no compelling evidence of speed-ups, and no measurable faster software delivery from non-technical users.

contract.note: Zitron gave no period; the January–March 2026 window was the evaluator's choice. 'There isn't compelling evidence' describes the evidence available at the time of the post, so leaving out earlier controlled studies on dates alone misreads that part. 'Compelling' also has no stated standard.

evidence.note: Block's February 2026 disclosure links a cut from about 10,000 to under 6,000 staff to AI tools. This is management's account; it does not independently show AI actually doing the work.
Guardian, March 2026. It confirms roughly 4,000 layoffs, while workers dispute that AI can do their jobs. Substitution remains unverified.

2025 trials across three companies with 4,867 developers found 26% more completed tasks. This is significant against the 'no compelling evidence' part, but it covers professional developers, predates the contract window, and is noisy.
METR, February 2026. Raw results show some speed-up, but METR calls the data unreliable because of selection effects. This settles neither side.

reviews.rationale: Not replacing anyone: Block's AI-linked cuts are management's account and disputed, so substitution is not verified. No compelling speed-up evidence: the 2025 trials challenge this but fall outside the window, and 'compelling' has no stated standard. Non-technical users: there is no qualifying study. No part is settled, and the period restriction is the evaluator's, not the speaker's.
